To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Landau potentials that include stress and temperature dependence of the elastic energy, and the chemical energy, are consistent with the phenomenology of martensitic transformations, and the phase field model that incorporates the Landau potentials, the effect of spatially oscillating fields and the effect of material inertia, is capable of describing the evolution of microstructures in martensitic transformations.

a Landau free energy with the phenomenology of a stress induced martensite transformation, and a diffuse interface with a finite athermal threshold, are sufficient to reproduce the observed microstructures and phase transformation hystereseis.
the introduction of an athermal interface threshold in a phase field model of martensitic phase transformation is equivalent to the introduction of a stress field that is oscillatory in space.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a phase field model for stress induced martensite phase transformations.
the development and analysis of phase field models for the simulation of martensitic transformations, with emphasis on the effect of stress and temperature on microstructure evolution.

the development of phase field models of stress induced phase transformations that account for the physics of the problem, and the development of efficient numerical methods to study the evolution of microstructures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
phase field models with spatially oscillatory driving fields and an athermal interface are capable of reproducing the phenomenology of martensitic phase transformation in a wide range of conditions.

the introduction of a threshold for the interface velocity, either by an analytic expression, or by the introduction of spatial oscillations in the driving force, allows one to obtain realistic stationary microstructures and rate independent phase transformation hysteresa.
the introduction of athermal effects in phase field models is necessary to reproduce rate independent temperature and mechanical hysteresis, and to obtain realistic stationary microstructures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inclusion of athermal friction in phase field simulations of stress induced martansitic phase transformations is essential to obtain physically realistic results.

we have shown that the introduction of a threshold in phase field models of martensitic phase transformation is essential for realistic microstructure evolution, and that the introduction of an athermal interface is more physically justified than an a priori threshold in the rate equations.
the introduction of an athermal friction in phase field simulations of martensitic transformations is essential in reproducing realistic microstructures and hysteresis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
athermal effects are necessary to capture the phenomenology of martensitic phase transformation.

the introduction of a spatially oscillatory field in the phase field model is an effective method to introduce an athermal threshold, and thus the effect of an elastic Peierls barrier in phase field models of martensitic transformations.

phase field models of stress induced phase transformations are capable of describing realistic microstructure evolution, provided that an athermal threshold for the interface propagation is introduced in a realistic way.
